info.desc: American Idiot is the seventh studio album by the American punk rock band Green Day. It was co-produced with longterm collaborator Rob Cavallo and released on September 21st, 2004 through Reprise Records. In mid-2003, the band began recording songs for an album titled Cigarettes and Valentines. However, the master tracks were lost and the band decided to start over rather than re-record Cigarettes and Valentines. They decided to produce a rock opera, inspired by the work of The Who and numerous musicals. It follows the life of "Jesus of Suburbia", a sort of anti-hero created by Billie Joe Armstrong. podcast.body: In the 21st century, Green Day made a significant return with an ultra-political concept album designed as a rock opera. This ambitious project successfully retained the band's pop punk sensibilities while redefining the genre through its serious thematic content. "Green Day roared back with an ultra-political concept album, Rock Opera, that nonetheless still kept their pop punk sensibilities intact."

srcs.episode: History of Pop Punk: Part 2

podcast.body: Marking a significant career comeback, this quasi-concept album emerged from Billie Joe Armstrong's strong feelings about George Bush's administration and overseas wars, after the mysterious disappearance of the master tapes for their previous project, "Cigarettes and Valentines." It exploded in popularity, generating half a dozen singles and selling 23 million copies worldwide, becoming the band's second-highest selling album after "Dookie." The album was a critical success, earning multiple Grammys, a Juno, an MTV Europe Music Award, and a Brit Award. It also inspired a successful stage musical that toured globally and a documentary titled "Heart Like a Hand Grenade," with Armstrong expressing hope for a future movie adaptation. "American Idiot was a global event, a cultural touchstone, and one of the last rock albums that we'll ever see selling these numbers."

podcast.body: Released in 2004, this 13-track punk rock opera served as a significant comeback album for Green Day, selling millions of copies rapidly. The album features a narrative involving characters like St. Jimmy and an unnamed narrator, exploring themes such as consumerism, paranoia, alienation, war, neurosis, and introspection. Its manager stated that a movie adaptation is a possibility, though it would require a skilled screenwriter. "Suddenly they were on to something and before anyone realized what was going on, Green Day had constructed a 13-track punk rock opera."

It exemplifies a later resurgence of social and political content within rock music, showing the enduring legacy of such themes. podcast.body: Released on September 21, 2004, this album, built from song snippets, became a highly successful rock opera. It sold 14 million copies, won Grammys, produced a DVD and live album, and a spin-off musical, cementing the band's renaissance and riding its success for over two years. "Green Day, a band whose time had come again thanks to the revival of rock that began in 2003, and they would ride the success of American Idiot for more than two years after its release on September 21, 2004."

"And the result of all that was the American Idiot album."

podcast.body: This album, released in the fall, was conceived as a full-blown rock opera. The band had fallen out of favor with fans and was perceived as "old and tired," with talk of their potential demise; this rock opera was considered a last-ditch effort to revive their career. Legend states that the album was an "accident," originating after the band lost master tapes for a planned record titled *Cigarettes and Valentines*. Instead of re-recording, they started from scratch, with each member contributing short fragments of music. These fragments sounded good together and, when strung into longer pieces, inspired the band to revisit older rock operas like those by The Who and Andrew Lloyd Webber's *Jesus Christ Superstar* for guidance. "An American idiot was actually an accident."
